paragraphs.source_en: “A woman calling herself Kaneda’s wife came just now asking about you.” The master explained this to Kangetsu in all seriousness. I seized the moment and secretly watched Kangetsu’s face, wondering whether he would be startled, pleased, or embarrassed. But he showed no particular change; once again he toyed with his purple cord and said in his usual calm tone, “I suppose she came to ask you to have me take her daughter as my wife.” “Not at all,” said Meitei. “That esteemed mother of hers is the owner of a magnificent nose...” Before Meitei could finish, the master suddenly broke in with a complete non sequitur: “I say, Meitei, I have been composing a haikai-style poem about that nose.” In the next room, the master’s wife could not help tittering. Meitei said, “You are remarkably carefree. Have you finished it?” “I have made a little of it. The first line is, ‘For this face, a festival of the nose.’” Meitei asked eagerly, “And then?” “Next comes: ‘To this nose, sacred wine is offered.’” “And the next line?” “That is as far as I have got.” “That is amusing,” said Kangetsu with a grin. Meitei immediately produced another line: “How about adding, ‘Two nostrils, dim and deep’?” Kangetsu followed with, “Might one not add, ‘So deep within, no hairs are seen’?” While the three of them were stringing together such nonsense, four or five people began shouting noisily in the road by the fence: “Imado-ware badger! Imado-ware badger!” The master and Meitei were startled and peered out through the fence. Then came a burst of laughter, followed by the sound of feet scattering into the distance. Meitei asked the master in puzzlement, “What does ‘Imado-ware badger’ mean?” The master replied, “I have no idea what it means.” Kangetsu observed, “They have quite a knack for invention.” Meitei, as if something had suddenly occurred to him, got to his feet and, in the tone of a lecture, said, “For many years I have studied this nose from the standpoint of aesthetics, and I should like to disclose a portion of my findings here, if you two gentlemen will favor me with your attention.” The master, dumbfounded by this sudden proposal, stared silently at Meitei. Kangetsu said softly, “By all means, I should like to hear it.” Meitei said, “I have investigated the matter in various ways, but I still cannot determine the precise origin of the nose. My first doubt is this: if we assume it to be a practical instrument, then two holes are quite sufficient; there is no need whatsoever for it to thrust itself out so arrogantly from the very middle of the face. And yet why, as you see, has it gradually risen and protruded to such a height?” As he said this, Meitei pinched his own nose by way of demonstration. The master said bluntly, “Your nose is hardly so very prominent.” “At any rate, it has not sunk in. But if you two gentlemen mistakenly regard my nose as merely two holes arranged side by side, misunderstanding may arise; I wish to warn you of that beforehand. Let me continue.

paragraphs.source_zh: “一个自称是金田老婆的女人，刚才打听你来啦。”主人认真地向寒月说明。我抓住时机，偷偷观察了一下寒月的表情是吃惊呢还是高兴，或是不好意思？结果他若无其事，又摆弄起他那紫色的挂穗，用他那一向沉稳的语调说：“大概是来托你们让我娶她的女儿吧。”迷亭说：“不。那位令堂大人有个伟大的鼻子……”主人不等迷亭说完，就驴唇不对马嘴地接了一句：“迷亭君，我刚才给那个鼻子想了一首俳体诗呢。”在隔壁，主人的妻子忍不住笑出声来。迷亭说：“你倒是真有闲心，做好了吗？”“想出了几句。第一句是‘为此颜举行鼻会’。”迷亭急着问道：“那下边的句子呢？”“接下去是：‘向此鼻敬献美酒’呗。”“再下一句呢？”“我只写出这两句。”寒月嘻嘻地笑着说：“真有意思。”迷亭立刻就想出了一句：“接下去是‘鼻孔一双何其深’，你看如何？”寒月接下去说：“我再接一句：‘鼻毛深邃实难见’，行不行？”他们三人正在东拉西扯地联句，就在这当儿，紧靠墙根处，四五个人吵吵嚷嚷地喊道：“陶瓷脸老狸精，陶瓷脸老狸精！”主人和迷亭吃了一惊，隔着篱笆向外看。这时听到哈哈的笑声，随后是向远处跑掉的脚步声。迷亭奇怪地问主人说：“陶瓷脸老狸精是什么意思？”主人回答说：“不懂这是什么意思。”寒月评论说：“难得他们想得出来。”迷亭不知想到了什么，突然站起来，用讲演的语调说：“鄙人从美学的角度对这种鼻子进行了研究，我愿意在这儿发表一部分，有烦两位听听。”主人对这种突如其来的提议有些发愣，一声不响地瞧着迷亭。寒月小声说：“务必请允许我洗耳恭听。”迷亭说：“我经过多方考察，对于鼻子的起源，还是不甚清楚。首先，我感到怀疑的是，假定它是实用道具，那么，只要有两个鼻孔就足够了，根本没有必要这样旁若无人地在面孔的正当中突出来。而且为什么如诸位所看到的，越来越高高地突起呢？”迷亭说着，抓了一下自己的鼻子来证明。主人毫不客气地说：“你的鼻子也不见得怎样高耸呀。”“反正并没有塌下去。不过你们两位如果错误地将我的鼻子只看成是排列着两个鼻孔，就可能产生误解，这点是我事先要提醒各位的。让我接着讲下去。
